title: Why pain persists after nerve injury

scenes.visual: Title: Why pain persists after nerve injury. Show a sensory neuron, spinal cord, immune cells and brain as the levels to be explored.

scenes.tts: After a nerve injury, pain can outlast the injury because the nervous system itself changes. Sensory neurons can fire without a stimulus. The spinal cord receives more excitation. Immune cells can sustain the sensitivity. These changes matter because persistent pain can reflect altered processing at several levels. It is more than an acute warning that keeps going. Each experiment measures a particular part of that change.

scenes.visual: Open on a nerve-injury label, then reveal sensory neuron, spinal cord and immune-cell panels. Animate spontaneous firing without an incoming stimulus, increased excitatory input in the cord, and immune-to-neuron signals. Headline: Persistent pain can reflect changed processing. Keep the nerve-injury scope visible; do not imply every pain condition has these mechanisms.

scenes.tts: Start with the first neuron. Cultured human sensory neurons from tumour surgery sometimes fired spontaneously. That firing was associated with the donors' radicular or neuropathic pain. This is an association in a dish. Rat studies also show spontaneous firing in uninjured neighbours after nerve injury. In other rat recordings, spinal neurons received more frequent excitatory synaptic events. That measures input to a neuron. It does not measure unpleasantness.

scenes.visual: Move through three separately labelled preparations: cultured human dorsal root ganglion neurons from tumour-surgery donors, uninjured neighbouring rat afferents after nerve injury, and spinal recordings in anaesthetized rats. Show firing without an applied stimulus and then denser excitatory synaptic events. Label the human result association in culture. Finish with Synaptic input is not unpleasantness. Use qualitative schematics, not invented data.

scenes.tts: Next, immune cells can change neuronal signalling. In nerve-injured rats, lowering P two X four receptors on spinal microglia reduced touch hypersensitivity. A separate rat study supplied a link to neurons. Microglia stimulated with A T P released B D N F. That shifted the anion reversal potential of lamina one neurons. Blocking B D N F signalling through track B reversed both the shift and the hypersensitivity. These are links in a pathway, in rats.

Blocking BDNF signalling through TrkB reversed both the shift and the hypersensitivity. These are links in a pathway, in rats.

scenes.visual: Show two distinct rat-study panels. First: injury-induced P2X4 on reactive spinal microglia; lowering P2X4 reduces tactile allodynia. Second: ATP-stimulated microglia release BDNF, which acts through TrkB on a lamina I neuron and shifts the anion reversal potential in a depolarizing direction. Blocking BDNF–TrkB reverses the shift and allodynia. Keep the separate studies and rat scope explicit.

scenes.tts: Now the brain. Brain circuits shape the unpleasant side of pain, and they also send signals back down. In rodent experiments, stimulating the anterior cingulate cortex strengthened spinal excitatory transmission. Descending control can facilitate signalling too. Keep the measurements apart. A withdrawal reflex is not the whole pain experience. More synaptic events cannot tell us how unpleasant a stimulus feels.

scenes.visual: Show brain circuits connected to spinal cord, then highlight the anterior cingulate cortex and descending facilitation. Label the evidence rodent experiments. Reuse the reflex-versus-affect comparison as a general measurement distinction, with separate reflex and unpleasant-experience labels. Do not show an amygdala tagging or silencing experiment, or numerical equivalence between synaptic input and unpleasantness.

scenes.tts: Finally, the immune route depends on the context. In the tested mice, a microglial inhibitor reversed hypersensitivity in males, but not females. Females appeared to use adaptive immune cells. Without those cells, the inhibitor worked. The route could switch. Compartment matters too. Depleting macrophages reduced hypersensitivity in both sexes of mice. The authors favoured ganglion macrophages, but could not exclude skin dendritic cells. These animal findings do not establish a fixed rule for men and women.

scenes.visual: Show the tested male and female mouse conditions, then female mice lacking adaptive immune cells, where sensitivity to the microglial inhibitor appears. Label the route conditional, not fixed. Switch from spinal microglia to ganglion macrophages: systemic depletion reduces hypersensitivity in both sexes; add a skin-dendritic-cell caveat because depletion affected those cells too. End with the multi-level processing map and Animal findings do not establish a fixed human sex rule.
End card: When pain persists. Hold the sensory-neuron, spinal, immune and brain map; retain the nerve-injury and preparation-specific scope.
